🏢 Is ServiceNow Only for Large Corporations?
When people hear ServiceNow, they often think:
10,000+ employees. Global enterprises. Large IT teams. Huge implementations.

But there is another way to look at it.
What if ServiceNow isn't about the size of the company?
What if it is about the complexity of the work?
A 200-person company can have:
Hundreds of employee requests
Multiple approval processes
Customer service operations
Onboarding and offboarding
Compliance requirements
IT assets and access management
Vendors and contracts
Repetitive manual workflows

The problem isn't necessarily volume.
It can be process complexity.

💡 The small-business opportunity
A small organization doesn't necessarily need a massive ServiceNow implementation.

It could start with one painful process.

For example:
Employee joins → HR request → Manager approval → IT account → Laptop → Application access → Security validation

Instead of emails, spreadsheets and Teams messages:
Request → Workflow → Automation → Notification → Tracking → Audit

Then expand.
One workflow → Multiple workflows → Enterprise platform

🤖 And AI changes the equation
Historically, ServiceNow could feel too complex for smaller organizations because implementation and administration required specialized expertise.

AI and automation could change that model.

The opportunity becomes:
ServiceNow + AI + Pre-built workflows + Managed services

Instead of hiring a large ServiceNow team, a small company could potentially consume ServiceNow capabilities through a managed, highly automated service model.

That creates an interesting entrepreneurial opportunity too.

A consultant doesn't necessarily have to sell:
“Let's implement ServiceNow.”

They could sell: “Let's eliminate your employee onboarding paperwork.”

Then expand from there.
🔥 A different perspective

The question shouldn't be: “Is my company big enough for ServiceNow?”

It should be: “Is my business process complex enough to benefit from ServiceNow?”

Because small company doesn't always mean simple company.

And with AI lowering the operational complexity of enterprise platforms, the ServiceNow opportunity may increasingly move down-market—from only large enterprises toward smaller, process-intensive organizations.

The future may not be ServiceNow for every company.

It may be ServiceNow for every company with the right problem.

“AI regulation will slow innovation.” I saw a CTO argue that on LinkedIn, and he’s raising a real concern. But it’s only half of the picture. Rules do add friction. They can make things slower, costlier, and more complicated.

But the conversation can’t stop at whether regulation exists, or whether a particular law applies to your company.

Maybe you’re a B2B technology company in Canada or the U.S., where there is no single comprehensive AI law in Canada or at the U.S. federal level, and a lot of AI decisions still sit across a mix of privacy, employment, consumer protection, sector-specific and state rules. The EU AI Act may not apply to your company either.

You still have to decide what you’re willing to build.

If you build an AI-enabled product that another business will buy, integrate, or depend on, your decisions don’t stay inside your product team. Your product may end up inside someone else’s hiring, lending, support, or operations. Your decisions become their risk.

And not every one of those decisions will be answered by a law. That’s where ethics comes in.

UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of AI gives us a set of values and principles to help think through those decisions.

The full set is in the image below, but a few of them raise questions that don’t always show up in the legal review:

→ Proportionality and Do No Harm: Should this use case exist at all, even if a customer asks for it?

→ Fairness and Non-Discrimination: Who could your product quietly work worse for?

→ Human Dignity: Behind every customer are people who never signed your contract. What does your product do to them?

These decisions get made in sprint planning meetings, product discussions and design choices, not only in legal reviews. You don’t need a regulator to see why they matter.

At some point, a company still has to decide what it is willing to do, even when no law is forcing the answer.

Under POPIA, your company is accountable for what your AI vendor does with your customers' data, wherever in the world that vendor processes it.

This week Bowmans (Law Firm) warned that making decisions about people based solely on AI can breach Section 71 of POPIA. Their warning was about hiring, but the same rule applies to any AI agent that decides something with real consequences for a customer, such as credit or cover, without a person involved.

Many buyers don't realise that a number of AI products sold under South African brands are wrappers, local labels on international platforms that process data offshore. To send personal information out of the country lawfully, they rely on Section 72 of POPIA. It allows transfers with consent, a binding agreement, an adequate foreign law or where the transfer is needed to perform a contract.

That route is legal when it's done properly. My question is whether it's the strongest and safest route for a business whose reputation rides on every customer conversation, and whether South African companies really want their customers' voices leaving the country to get there.

Do you know which country your AI vendor processes your customers' calls in? 

If the Information Regulator asked you for that answer tomorrow, how long would it take you to produce it?

We are moving Untapped AI's compute into South African data centres and building our own voice models locally, because we believe sovereign infrastructure will become the standard for AI that speaks to South Africans.

CIOs and compliance officers, I'd value your view in the comments...

“Why should I pay someone to write my resume? ChatGPT or Claude can do it for free.”

Fair question.

But here’s the problem:
AI can write a resume.
It cannot automatically know what your career should be positioned as.

I recently worked with three very different professionals:
🔹 21+ years | Automotive Quality
Powertrain, Gearbox, Engine, Machining, Heat Treatment, Assembly, IATF, Plant Quality.
🔹 17+ years | Pharma & Biotech Packaging
Vaccines, Biotherapeutics, Animal Health, Contract Manufacturing and international markets across Europe, Canada, Australia, India and more.
🔹 38+ years | Business & Commercial Leadership
Building Materials, Ceramics, Sanitaryware and Luminaries. Progressed from Management Trainee to Vice President. Led 250–300 people across multiple South Indian markets.

Now imagine asking AI:
“Write a professional resume for me.”
It can produce a polished document.

But will it know that:
❌ The 21-year Quality professional should not be positioned merely as a “Quality Engineer”?
❌ The 17-year Packaging professional's international market exposure needs to be brought forward—not buried under technical responsibilities?
❌ The 38-year professional needs to be positioned as a Business & Commercial Leader, rather than someone with a very long list of job responsibilities?

That is the difference.

A resume is not about putting everything you have done on paper.
It is about deciding:
What should the recruiter notice first?
What should be quantified?
What should be removed?
Which achievements establish seniority?
Which keywords align with the target role?
Which part of 20+ years of experience is actually relevant today?
And most importantly:
What story does your career tell?

Because here's the uncomfortable truth:
If 1,000 candidates are using AI to create resumes, a beautifully written AI resume is no longer a differentiator.

It becomes the baseline.

The differentiation comes from strategy + relevance + key contributions + positioning.
AI is a powerful tool. I use AI too.

But I don't believe in giving AI a career history and saying:
“Make this resume.”

First comes the human work:
Understand the professional → identify the target → extract the right achievements → quantify impact → build the positioning → then use technology where it adds value.

Because your resume shouldn't merely answer:
“What have you done?”

It should answer:
“Why should a recruiter consider you for THIS role?”

AI can write your resume but your career deserves more than a generic prompt.

"Your Resume is not your biography.
It is your Sales Pitch."

Comment "Resume" and I'll share a professionally crafted resume with strategic positioning and you'll be able to see the difference.

Wipro just said something big. AI didn't take jobs. It gave people new ones. Let that sink in for a moment. AI didnt knock on the door to take jobs away.

It walked in quietly and made room for people to grow.

I've been reading about this, and I think it says a lot about where we are headed. This comes at a time when Indias $315 billion software services industry is dealing with AI in a big way. Its changing how companies hire, build software, and even sign contracts.

Here's what stood out to me from Wipro CTO Sandhya Ramachandran Arun's interview:

📍Wipro has about 243,000 employees as of June.

📍The company is moving to a "human-AI operating model." In simple words - humans and AI work side by side.

📍Over 100,000 employees have already got advanced AI training and certifications.

📍The freed-up capacity is not cut. It is moved to new projects and new roles.

Now let me tell you the bigger industry picture I'm seeing. Tata Consultancy Services India's largest software exporter, said back in June that hiring will slow down.

Why? Because they want an equal number of employees and AI agents in their workforce.

TCS is also building a team of up to 8,900 forward-deployed engineers. Infosys plans for about 6,000 over the next few years. These engineers sit directly with clients to help them adopt AI faster.

So the pattern is clear to me. Every big IT company is reshaping its workforce around AI, just in different ways.

The real question I keep asking myself is this: as AI keeps freeing up capacity, will companies use it to grow and hire for new skills? Or will teams just get smaller over time?

At TalentOnLease, we are watching this shift closely.

What do you think - is this the safest way to bring in AI, or just the calm before a bigger change?

A few days ago, I received an email from Mercor that caught my attention.

 “You’ve received an instant work offer for Multimodal Image Expert - Assessment.” 

The interesting part? I didn't apply directly for the role. 

Mercors matching system surfaced my profile based on previous assessments and experience, and after reviewing my profile, the hiring manager agreed that I was a strong fit.

I accepted the contract. For me, this was more than just another work offer. It made me pause and think about the progress Ive made over the past few years.

I started out doing data annotation, learning how important accuracy, consistency, attention to detail, and following guidelines are when working with AI data. 

Over time, that work grew into LLM evaluation, annotation QA, edge-case analysis, and reviewing AI-generated outputs across different types of data. 

I've had to learn not just how to annotate data, but how to question it. Is this label actually correct? 

Did the model interpret this correctly? Does this output follow the guideline? What happens in this edge case? 
Can this process be improved? 

That shift from simply completing tasks to thinking about quality, accuracy, and how AI systems interpret data has been one of the biggest parts of my growth. 

Now, seeing opportunities like a Multimodal Image Expert role come through is a reminder that the small skills you build consistently can eventually open doors to more specialized work. 

I'm still learning, still improving, and still building my experience in AI data quality and evaluation.

But Im also learning to appreciate the progress. 

One project, one assessment, one dataset, one QA review at a time. 

The goal isnt just to work with AI. Its to become better at understanding, evaluating, and improving the data that helps AI work better. On to the next one.

Reading Richard Harris's post this morning on what “Legal 500 firms can learn from Michelin-starred restaurants” sent me down a rabbit hole about my own industry.

Richard's point, that in a world where the technical craft is already excellent and AI is levelling it further, the real differentiator becomes understanding the person on the other side of the table, lands squarely in recruitment too. A lot of what recruiters have historically been paid for is now being done by software. Sourcing, matching, screening, scheduling, first-draft outreach. AI will keep eating that layer. And maybe it should (maybe it shouldn't), most of it was never where the value lived anyway.

The value has always been in the context.

Knowing that a candidate's real motivation isn't the salary bump, it's the chance to build something of their own. Hearing what a hiring manager isn't saying about the team they've inherited. Understanding that the "non-negotiable" on the brief is actually negotiable, and the real deal-breaker is a cultural pattern nobody has named out loud yet. That's not a database query. That's judgement, earned through relationships.

And this is where it ties back to the work I do, on the compliance and governance side of the industry through The ORARA Group. My context isn't just what makes a great placement, it's what makes a defensible one. Every recruitment business has a different risk appetite. Different clients, different sectors, different regulatory exposure, different tolerance for grey areas. A framework that's proportionate for a life sciences executive search boutique would strangle a high-volume contract desk, and vice versa.

Good compliance, like good recruitment, isn't about applying a template. It's about understanding what this business is actually trying to achieve, what it's genuinely worried about, and where its leaders are putting their own judgement and credibility on the line. Then building something that fits.

AI can draft the policy. AI can flag the anomaly. AI cannot tell you whether this client, in this market, with this team, should say yes to that piece of business. That still takes a human who has bothered to understand you.

Richard said that “sometimes the thing that makes the difference is the baked beans”. In recruitment and in compliance, I'd call it the same thing, it's the discipline of actually listening before you serve.

Thanks to Richard Harris, for his original post, it is well worth a read.

After I posted about my son's rescinded offer, a friend called with his own version.

His son landed a contract job at a major bank. He did the paperwork and the online training and went to orientation on a Thursday. His start date was Monday. On Friday the bank cancelled the whole program.

Nobody said AI caused either one, and I don't know that it did. But the pattern is hard to miss. At companies that adopted generative AI, junior hiring fell about 9 percent within six quarters. Senior jobs didn't move.

Here is what worries me as an operator. Nobody ever paid a first year analyst for the reconciliation. They paid for the person that two years of reconciliations would produce. The grunt work was the apprenticeship.

Cut it and you haven't cut a cost. You've cut the process that builds your future partners. In healthcare it's the coder who spends five years learning why claims get denied and becomes your revenue cycle director.

The class of 2026 will find its way. The class of 2036 is the one I'd worry about.

Keep the entry class. Rewrite the junior jobs instead of deleting them.

AI is the rain. Ethics is the umbrella. The umbrella doesn't stop the rain, but it decides whether you arrive at your destination soaked or ready to work.

AI already writes our emails, screens our CVs, routes our shipments, and flags our mistakes. The question now is whether we're using it with our eyes open. 

Using AI ethically isn't a policy document you sign once and forget. It's a set of small decisions you make every day. Here are the ones I think matter most. 

Be transparent. 
If AI helped make a decision that affects someone, like a loan, a hiring shortlist, or a price, that person deserves to know. Hiding the machine behind the decision erodes trust faster than any mistake the machine makes. 

Protect the data. 
This one is simple and still widely ignored. If data needed protecting before AI, it needs even more protection now. Pasting customer records or confidential contracts into a public chatbot isn't a productivity hack. It's a data leak with extra steps. 

Check for bias. 
AI learns from the past, and the past wasn't always fair. A model trained on yesterday's hiring decisions will happily repeat yesterday's prejudices at scale. Someone has to ask whom it might leave out. Keep a human accountable. The algorithm decided is not an answer. Every AI system needs a named person who owns its outcomes, can explain them, and can switch it off. 

Verify before you trust. 
AI can be confidently, fluently wrong. Hallucinated facts, fake citations, and invented numbers are real risks. Treat its output like a first draft from a bright but overconfident intern. 

Stay vigilant. 
The same tools that help us also help attackers. Deepfake voices asking finance teams to wire money, phishing emails with perfect grammar, and synthetic identities are already here. Security awareness has to catch up. None of this means slowing down. 

Organizations that build trust into their AI now will move faster later, because their customers, regulators, and employees will believe them.

Lately, I have noticed a deeply concerning trend in technical recruitment, especially targeting senior systems, engine, and game developers working with C++, Rust, and various Game Engines.

Platforms are reaching out with high-paying, short-term offers for AI evaluation projects. The catch is always the same. Before a single interview is scheduled, and before any NDA or contract is signed, you are asked to submit your repository links, playable builds, and a 5-minute video walkthrough explaining your architectural choices, memory management, and engineering workflows.

Let's call this what it actually is. This isn't a traditional hiring funnel. It is mass data harvesting disguised as a job application.

The tech giants behind frontier AI models (like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta) have a massive problem right now. They have already scraped the entire public internet and exhausted open-source platforms, but their models still struggle with high-level logic. Now, they are desperately trying to lay their hands on proprietary work and internal engineering reasoning.

When you record a video breaking down your code, you are giving away the holy grail of AI training, which is expert human feedback (RLHF). You are teaching a future model exactly how a senior engineer thinks, and you are doing it completely for free with zero guarantees of employment.

However, there is no such thing as free lunch. If these corporations want to train their models on our real-world engineering processes, they need to hire us as legitimate contractors and pay for every single repository and video session we provide. We cannot allow our years of expertise to be devalued just so a handful of AI companies can maximize their profit margins.

Personally, this pervasive data grabbing has forced me to completely alter my workflow to protect my intellectual property. Due to widespread unauthorized scraping and aggressive recruitment tactics, I actually had to remove my public repositories from GitHub and other open platforms to safeguard my IP.

On top of that, I stopped using cloud-based AI coding assistants because they treat every single line of user input as free training data. Instead, I now rely exclusively on offline, locally hosted models that I often have to fine-tune myself to meet the demands of advanced systems programming.

We need to protect our code and our engineering judgment. Your expertise is worth a premium, and it should never be given away under the pressure of a rushed application deadline. If a platform demands your IP upfront without a contract, just walk away.
